arguments.name: Eight early lines of evidence support the resurrection
arguments.conclusion: There are eight separate lines of evidence, all accepted by critics, from the death of Jesus to the end of Paul's epistles, supporting the resurrection.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Critics date Paul's epistles from 50 to 60 AD, with 1 Thessalonians at about 50 and Mark at about 40.
P2: The four most important arguments show early eyewitnesses from the death of Jesus up to just six years.

P3: The four arguments covered are: the preaching started immediately, the creeds came from Jerusalem within 1-2 years, Paul was converted 2-3 years later, and Paul met Peter and James about six years after the cross.
P4: There are four more steps beyond these, all allowed by critics, before even considering the Gospel data.

st1.quote: There are eight separate lines of evidence all accepted by the critics from the death of Jesus to the end of Paul's epistles which would be just a little bit after.

st2.quote: The four most important arguments that say we have early eyewitnesses from the death of Jesus up until just six years.

st3.quote: Gerd Lüdemann, prominent New Testament scholar, he said that when Jesus died, the preaching of the gospel message actually the preaching of the resurrection message started immediately.

st4.quote: But by 25 approximately eight separate arguments.

st5.quote: You might say, "Well, already I'm wondering why they don't admit the resurrection." Most people don't believe because the facts tell them to believe. Most people have world-view beliefs that give them their beliefs more than anything else.

st6.quote: I could give you a list of atheists, agnostics, non-Christians, they call themselves self-proclaimed non-Christians, and skeptics who will grant all eight of them.

st7.quote: How do you know we don't have homologia and creeds and Paul's testimony, but it's telephone tag?

st8.quote: By just 6 years later, by 6 years later, we've got the earliest preaching started right away. Everybody admits that. From the apostolic church in Jerusalem. Secondly, you've got the the sunflower seed, the kernel, the creeds. Next, you've got Paul's conversion. And lastly, he goes up to Jerusalem and has his gospel message affirmed by the others.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, minimal facts argument / 'The Historical Jesus' (1980s-2000s); also Habermas, 'On the Resurrection' (2024).

or1.quote: There are eight separate lines of evidence all accepted by the critics from the death of Jesus to the end of Paul's epistles
or1.why: It is a compressed variant of Habermas's own minimal-facts approach, organized as eight critic-accepted steps.

or2.quote: the earliest agreed-upon data in the early church had to do with the gospel preaching
or2.why: It brings the homologia/creed distinction and the Galatians 1-2 historesai detail as fresh support, but not a new class of evidence.

or3.quote: What kind of sources do we have for Alexander the Great?
or3.why: It adds a cross-domain comparison with Alexander and Buddha source-dating, a rhetorical bridge rather than a new historical argument.

or4.quote: There are eight separate lines of evidence all accepted by the critics
or4.why: No formalization, equation or model is added; it is a numbered list.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from critic-accepted dates and creeds to 'eight separate lines of evidence' is not shown to be independent or to entail the resurrection.
arguments.develop_next: Specify each of the eight steps with its critic source and show they are independent, then state what would falsify the chain.

arguments.name: Most doubt is emotional, not factual
arguments.conclusion: The great majority of doubts Christians experience are emotional rather than factual, so factual evidence alone will not resolve them.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: Habermas and a clinical psychologist gave people a psychological battery of tests about their doubts.
P2: The great majority of doubts are not factual but emotional.
P3: Emotional doubt often involves 'what if' questions with no evidence behind them.
P4: Emotional doubt hurts because it concerns one's most important relationship and salvation.
P5: Answering an emotional doubter with data will not work; one must deal with the emotions and tell them where to get off.

st1.quote: the great majority of doubts are not factual, but they're emotional

st2.quote: He gave people a psychological battery of tests, asked questions about the doubts they had ever since they've been Chris- Christians.

st3.quote: He gave people a psychological battery of tests, asked questions about the doubts they had ever since they've been Chris- Christians. And the great majority of doubts are not factual, but they're emotional.

st4.quote: if you answer an emotional doubter with data, it won't work

st6.quote: the great majority of doubts are not factual, but they're emotional

st8.quote: Talk to a lot of women. Um minister people come up questions and almost every single time I ask a woman, "Why do you like apologetics?"

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, 'The Thomas Factor' / books on doubt (1990s-2000s); Os Guinness, 'God in the Dark' (1996).

or1.quote: I have three books on doubt
or1.why: It restates Habermas's own published thesis on doubt with added clinical-testing detail.

or2.quote: We This took us years. He did most of the work. He gave people a psychological battery of tests
or2.why: It cites a psychological battery of tests, data the prior devotional literature does not use.

or3.quote: It's often, as we were talking before, it's often a gender thing.
or3.why: It connects apologetics to clinical psychology and gender, a modest cross-domain link.

or4.why: No formal model or structure is offered.

arguments.weakest_link: The claim that a 'great majority' of doubts are emotional rests on an unnamed study with no reported sample, questions or results.
arguments.develop_next: Report the actual battery, sample and percentages, and give criteria for distinguishing emotional from factual doubt.

arguments.name: 80% of early creeds center on death and resurrection
arguments.conclusion: About 80% of the homologia and creeds in the New Testament center on the death and resurrection of Jesus, showing God wanted that to be the central message.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: About 80% of the homologia and creeds in the New Testament are about the death and resurrection of Jesus.
P2: They do not focus on disputed topics like Old Testament genocide, the time of creation, the last days, sovereignty and free will, or Calvinism versus non-Calvinism.
P3: The most heated topics Christians disagree about are not the fundamentals.
P4: There is agreement on the fundamentals, and 80% of these sources center on the gospel.

st1.quote: about 80% of them in the New Testament are about 80% death and resurrection of Jesus

st2.quote: Why don't they talk about so-called Old Testament genocide? Why don't they talk about what's the time of creation?

st4.quote: I think God wanted us to know what it was.

st6.quote: I think God wanted us to know what it was.

st8.quote: But, there's agreement on the fundamentals and 80% of these sources are on this center.

arguments.prior_art: None known (the 80% homologia/creed statistic appears to be Habermas's own).

or1.quote: about 80% of them in the New Testament are about 80% death and resurrection of Jesus
or1.why: I know no prior work making this specific statistical claim about the creeds.

or2.quote: The homologia and the creeds about 80% of them in the New Testament are about 80% death and resurrection of Jesus.
or2.why: It introduces a quantitative claim about creed content that the prior art does not use.

or3.quote: The most heated topics we disagree about are not the fundamentals as a general rule.
or3.why: It links creed statistics to ecclesial disputes, a mild cross-domain move.

or4.why: No formalization is given for the 80% figure.

arguments.weakest_link: The 80% figure is asserted without any count, sample or definition of which texts count as homologia/creeds.
arguments.develop_next: Publish the list and coding rules behind the 80% figure so it can be checked and reproduced.

arguments.name: Paul's conclusion calls for steadfastness and fruitful labor
arguments.conclusion: Because Christ is raised, believers should be steadfast, labor in the Lord is not in vain, and death and the devil are defeated.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: P1: 1 Corinthians 15:58 says 'be steadfast,' which means stand firm, don't give up, don't walk away.
P2: Paul says your labor in the Lord is not in vain; good works do not save, but post-salvation works determine the capacity to enjoy eternity.
P3: Even a cup of cold water given in the name of a disciple will not lose its reward.
P4: Paul quotes the Old Testament: 'Death, where is your sting? Grave, where is your victory?'
P5: Paul is trash-talking death and the devil because the empty tomb means they have lost their prized possession.
P6: If Christ has not been raised, let us eat and drink for tomorrow we die; but Christ has been raised, so believers are victors now and forever.

st2.quote: He said, "Keep up with your good works. They're not in vain."

st3.quote: He says, "Even a cold cup of water given in the name of a disciple will not lose its reward."

st4.quote: If Christ has not been raised, let us eat and drink for tomorrow we die; but Christ has been raised, so believers are victors now and forever.

st6.quote: What you do with Jesus after salvation determines the capacity to which you will enjoy eternity.

st7.quote: He said if Christ is not been raised from the dead, let us eat and drink for tomorrow we die.

st8.quote: Paul says, quoting the Old Testament. You think he's probably quoting the '60s, but he's quoting the Old Testament.

arguments.prior_art: Standard Reformed/evangelical exposition of 1 Corinthians 15:58 (e.g. Charles Hodge, 1 Corinthians commentary, 1857); no single distinctive work.

or1.why: It is essentially the standard pulpit application of 1 Corinthians 15:58 restated.

or2.why: It brings no new premise, evidence or data beyond the biblical text.

or4.why: No formalization or model is added.

arguments.weakest_link: The move from 'Christ is raised' to specific rewards and degrees of eternal enjoyment is asserted, not argued.
arguments.develop_next: Give the exegetical argument linking 1 Corinthians 15:58 and its context to the reward claim, and address the main alternative reading.
